Because of COVID-19 , &amp;ldquo ; I can&amp;rsquo ; t do that right now . I haven&amp;rsquo ; t been able to do that for three or four months . I have a whole team of people sitting in my lab , unable to directly assess patients , &amp;rdquo ; said the renowned Western University neuroscientist who has devoted much of his career searching for signs of consciousness and awareness in unresponsive patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But then the crisis started escalating ; reports starting to come in of people suffering neurological consequences , and it became apparent to Owen about six or eight weeks ago &amp;ldquo ; that if we&amp;rsquo ; re ever going to understand this , this is something we need to do , now . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What he&amp;rsquo ; s doing now is launching a massive study to explore the impacts of COVID-19 on the brain . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The online &lt;a href= " https : **33;2626;TOOLONG ... Brain Study&lt;/a&gt; aims to recruit 50,000 people with a confirmed , positive diagnosis of the virus . Using questionnaires and pop down menus , Owen and his collaborators will collect information , &amp;ldquo ; completely anonymized and secure , &amp;rdquo ; asking participants about their medical history , any underlying heart , lung or other health issues , the extent of their COVID-19 diagnosis and what happened to them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They&amp;rsquo ; ll be asked to perform cognitive games that assess memory , decision-making , planning and problem solving , and results will be compared against a huge database of millions of tests completed by a healthy , normal population . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For the study , Owen has partnered with Sunnybrook Hospital stroke neurologist Dr. Rick Swartz . They&amp;rsquo ; re hoping for a large and diverse group ( the study is available in English , French and Spanish ) . They hope that with 50,000 people they&amp;rsquo ; ll have enough statistical power to tease apart &amp;ldquo ; all of these little nuances , &amp;rdquo ; Owen said , and answer questions like , are there certain proportions of the population that are more vulnerable to developing cognitive deficits &amp;mdash ; fuzzy thinking , brain fog , problems concentrating ? The new virus shares many of the same features as its more lethal predecessor . Both use spike proteins to bind to a protein called ACE2 on the surface of &amp;ldquo ; host , &amp;rdquo ; in this case human host , cells , and some scientists have found ACE2 receptors scattered through the brain , on neurons as well as the star-shaped glial cells that help nourish them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The virus might also invade the brain by several routes , the review article found , including&amp;nbsp ; via the olfactory nerve , which might explain why people with COVID-19 so frequently report loss of taste and smell . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other common neurologic complaints in COVID-19 include headache , stroke , impaired consciousness , seizure and encephalopathy. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This virus is new ; there&amp;rsquo ; s no long-term data on people who have recovered from COVID-19. &amp;ldquo ; But there are plenty of reports of people reporting what in a clinical context we refer to as delirium , &amp;rdquo ; Owen said . &amp;ldquo ; There are people coming out of the ICU recovering from COVID and saying they don&amp;rsquo ; t feel themselves . And this is sort of the typical profile that we know goes on to produce long-term consequences . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; High doses of some sedatives in the ICU can contribute to delirium , a kind of brain dysfunction that can lead to a serious state of confusion and even paranoid delusions that the brain lays down as &amp;ldquo ; real&amp;rdquo ; memories . Holmes : A little leak can lead to big problemshttp : **32;3068;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **33;3102;TOOLONG ... title= " Look for signs of leaks around fixtures , faucets , and appliances , Mike Holmes advises . " alt= " Look for signs of leaks around fixtures , faucets , and appliances , Mike Holmes advises . " data-portal-copyright= " Photo Alex Schuldtz , The Holmes Group " **28;3137;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78576844 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Often when I talk about leaky homes , I talk about the big stuff : Leaks that come in through your outdoor structure , like the roof , windows , or foundation . While these can cause a major of water damage , sometimes , the leak can be coming from inside the house . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; You&amp;rsquo ; ve got a whole host of pipes and plumbing hiding behind your walls that could be slowly leaking &amp;mdash ; either due to age , improper install , or an unfortunate accident like a burst pipe . Even if you&amp;rsquo ; ve taken every step to prevent water from sneaking in through your building envelope , you&amp;rsquo ; re not totally safe from water damage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Here are a few places to keep an eye out for leaks : &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Is it in the kitchen ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A plumbing leak can be a common source of costly water bills . Even a small leak can add up to big bills over time . Where should you be on the hunt for leaks ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Look for standing water at the bottom of your dishwasher . Check where the dishwasher connects to the main drain . You&amp;rsquo ; re looking for signs of discoloration on the hose to indicate a water leak . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Faucets and fixtures don&amp;rsquo ; t last forever , especially if you bought cheap ones . If the unit is still dripping after it&amp;rsquo ; s shut off , you&amp;rsquo ; ve got a leak . You may also see discoloration around the base of the fixtures or in the sink cabinetry caused by water damage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If it&amp;rsquo ; s a small leak , you could try fixing it yourself . For compression faucets ( faucets where you tighten the washer to stop water flow ) , the No. 1 cause is a worn-out washer or O-ring . These are pretty simple to replace , but you MUST replace it with an exact fit or you will still have a leak . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For cartridge faucets ( which typically use an up and down function , rather than a twist function ) , you can try replacing the cartridge in the unit . Again , you&amp;rsquo ; ll need the exact size to make a successful replacement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Is it in the bathroom ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Everything I&amp;rsquo ; ve already mentioned about faucets and fixtures remains true for the bathroom , though with one note of caution . If the leak is in the shower or tub , it could be a sign of something bigger going on behind the walls . That is a job I&amp;rsquo ; d leave to a pro . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are two types of toilet leaks . It could either be due to the flush valve for the fill valve . If the flush valve doesn&amp;rsquo ; t form a watertight seal , overtime water will begin to leak into the toilet ball . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When the fill valve isn&amp;rsquo ; t fitted properly , either it&amp;rsquo ; s placed too high , or doesn&amp;rsquo ; t close properly , the tank will experience constant flowing water into overflow tube . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Silent toilet leaks can waste upwards of 1,000 litres of water per day &amp;mdash ; so if you suspect a leak , call in a plumber quickly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Is it in the basement ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Look around your water heater for signs of leakage . You might see some rust spots , or some pooling water on the floor . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are a few reasons a water heater may leak , but the most common is a loose drain valve . You can try tightening it until it&amp;rsquo ; s snug and see if that does the trick . If the temperature was set too high , it could be creating too much pressure in the unit , also causing a leak . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Finally , the leak could be due to a cracked storage tank . Unfortunately , in that case , it&amp;rsquo ; s time to replace the unit . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Generally , if the water heater is leaking , it&amp;rsquo ; s still safe to use , but I recommend calling an expert quickly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A leaking washing machine could be caused by bad tub fittings , insecure supply hoses , or the internal hoses could be faltering . Checking the supply hoses and ensuring they&amp;rsquo ; re still firmly connected is pretty simple for any homeowner . But if you&amp;rsquo ; ve determined the leak is coming from inside the machine , your best bet is to have a pro look at it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A smart automatic water shut-off valve system can help you in the case of big leaks or a burst pipe . Health Ontario suffered exodus of senior leaders and budget cuts before the COVID-19 pandemic struckhttp : **34;4690;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **33;4726;TOOLONG ... title= " Ontario Premier Doug Ford , Minister of Health Christine Elliott and Ontario Chief Medical Officer of Health Dr. David Williams attend a news conference at the Ontario Legislature in Toronto on March 16 , 2020. " alt= " Ontario Premier Doug Ford , Minister of Health Christine Elliott and Ontario Chief Medical Officer of Health Dr. David Williams attend a news conference at the Ontario Legislature in Toronto on March 16 , 2020. " data-portal-copyright= " Frank Gunn / The Canadian Press " **28;4761;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78576649 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thirteen years ago , Dr. Natasha Crowcroft , a Cambridge-trained physician and expert in infectious disease surveillance , moved to Toronto from London to help rebuild Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s public health system after SARS . For 11 years , Crowcroft worked inside the agency known as &lt;a href= " https : **29;4791;TOOLONG " rel= " noopener " target= " blank " &gt;Public Health Ontario&lt;/a&gt; ( PHO ) in a series of progressively more senior roles . During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic , she led the agency&amp;rsquo ; s surveillance epidemiology group . Last year , in April , she was named PHO&amp;rsquo ; s chief science officer and senior scientist . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The public health system Crowcroft found in &lt;a href= " https : **31;4822;TOOLONG " rel= " noopener " target= " blank " &gt;Ontario&lt;/a&gt; was &amp;ldquo ; a bit of a dog&amp;rsquo ; s breakfast , &amp;rdquo ; she said . Over the years , there were constant squabbles between the Ministry of Health and PHO about issues like jurisdiction and independence . Crowcroft wasn&amp;rsquo ; t shocked by any of that . To an extent , it just goes with the territory in her field . &amp;ldquo ; Governments really don&amp;rsquo ; t like independent public health organizations that evaluate what&amp;rsquo ; s going on and tell them when they&amp;rsquo ; re not doing things right , &amp;rdquo ; she said . They&amp;rsquo ; re constantly trying to trim their wings and pull them back into the cage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I sometimes say it&amp;rsquo ; s a bit like the Death Star in Star Wars , &amp;rdquo ; Crowcroft said . &amp;ldquo ; You know you have to do everything you can not to get sucked into the tractor beam . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For all her frustrations , Crowcroft enjoyed working in public health . She thinks it&amp;rsquo ; s vitally important work , and interesting too . But two years ago , after the election of Doug Ford&amp;rsquo ; s Progressive Conservative government , the situation at Public Health Ontario , and in the Ontario public health system at large , began to deteriorate , she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ford government quickly froze PHO&amp;rsquo ; s budget and signalled that deeper cuts , to PHO and local health units , were on the way . The new administration also proved uninterested in some core public health missions , things like basic science . ? That hostility isn&amp;rsquo ; t entirely new . Some of it predates this government . &amp;ldquo ; But it did get worse under this government , &amp;rdquo ; Crowcroft said . &amp;ldquo ; The government has made it almost impossible for science to function within a public health organization . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t just science , either . Public Health Ontario was set up as an independent agency as a response to Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s failures during SARS . Crowcroft was specifically recruited to help with that effort . But the new government didn&amp;rsquo ; t want to hear about that part of PHO&amp;rsquo ; s history and mission , according to Crowcroft. &amp;ldquo ; The other message that was around before this happened was that people were saying , &amp;lsquo ; Don&amp;rsquo ; t talk about SARS anymore . The government doesn&amp;rsquo ; t want to hear about SARS , &amp;rdquo ; she said , &amp;ldquo ; which is supremely ironic right now . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hayley Chazan , a spokeswoman for Health Minister Christine Elliott , said in an email that that direction &amp;ldquo ; was never provided by the office of the minister of health . &amp;rdquo ; She also pointed to numerous ways the &lt;a href= " https : **33;4855;TOOLONG ... rel= " noopener " target= " blank " &gt;lessons learned from SARS&lt;/a&gt; have guided the provincial response to &lt;a href= " https : **32;4890;TOOLONG " rel= " noopener " target= " blank " &gt;COVID-19&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last summer , Crowcroft left Public Health Ontario to head up a new Centre for Vaccine Preventable Diseases at the University of Toronto . In June , she joined the World Health Organization . She hasn&amp;rsquo ; t been replaced at PHO . Her old job , chief scientist , no longer appears in the agency&amp;rsquo ; s leadership chart . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Crowcroft wasn&amp;rsquo ; t alone , either . In the year before the &lt;a href= " https : **33;4924;TOOLONG ... rel= " noopener " target= " blank " &gt;COVID-19 pandemic&lt;/a&gt; struck , Public Health Ontario lost a host of senior leaders in crucial roles . Some were pushed out due to budget constraints or organizational restructuring . Others took early retirement . Some were replaced . Many were not . &amp;ldquo ; I think there was maybe one person who was probably going to retire anyway , &amp;rdquo ; said Crowcroft. &amp;ldquo ; But my impression from the people I do know is an overwhelming majority were not necessarily planning to go at that time . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The loss of all that leadership , expertise and experience left Public Health Ontario undermanned in several areas crucial to pandemic response as the SARS-CoV-2 virus began to sweep the province earlier this year , according to multiple former senior PHO officials . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The province has been repeatedly criticized for its efforts on data collection and sharing during the pandemic . In early June , the government appointed former federal Liberal cabinet minister Dr. Jane Philpott as a special advisor on data in an effort to clean up the problem . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But until last year , Public Health Ontario had its own senior-level expert on data collection , presentation and sharing . Julian Martalog was hired as PHO&amp;rsquo ; s first director of informatics in 2016. &amp;ldquo ; My role was really just to make sure the organization had a way of transforming all the data they were collecting into information and knowledge , &amp;rdquo ; he said . Martalog was laid off last year . He hasn&amp;rsquo ; t been replaced . His position no longer appears on PHO&amp;rsquo ; s leadership chart . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think it was a little bit strange that they decided to eliminate that role in particular , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; I like to think that with this situation now , I would have been able to continue to make an impact and provide strong leadership , but it is what it is. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Martalog has watched the provincial pandemic response with some unease and confusion . &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsquo ; s stuff that comes out every day that makes me scratch my head , &amp;rdquo ; he said . He doesn&amp;rsquo ; t understand why critical information on things like deaths , infection rates and locations hasn&amp;rsquo ; t been better presented and easier to access . He believes that , if he was still at PHO , he could have made a difference . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I would have been heavily involved in that whole effort just to make sure that the right information is presented in a timely way , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Communication in general has been a sore spot for the province during the pandemic . Premier Ford and Chief Medical Officer of Health David Williams have at times presented conflicting messages in back-to-back to press conferences . Williams in particular has come under fire for his dry and sometimes convoluted delivery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ironically , Public Health Ontario had one of the country&amp;rsquo ; s leading experts on what&amp;rsquo ; s known as &amp;ldquo ; &lt;a href= " https : **33;4959;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;risk communication&lt;/a&gt; &amp;rdquo ; on staff until the end of March . Dr. Ray Copes was the agency&amp;rsquo ; s chief of environmental and occupational health . Part of his job was to train other public health units and officials on how to speak to the public about health risks and crises in ways that are coherent , calming and easy to absorb . There is no one left in the agency with that level of expertise , according to one senior official still in public health . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Copes&amp;rsquo ; departure from PHO was planned last year . But his final day on the job wasn&amp;rsquo ; t until the end of March , when the pandemic was already in full flight . He wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t say specifically why he left or if he was asked by PHO to stay on until the crisis waned . But he did say this about the general situation at the top of his former workplace : &amp;ldquo ; There certainly are some folks that aren&amp;rsquo ; t there anymore , who I think really could have made a contribution to the response had that been requested , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m not aware that that was done in the case of Public Health Ontario . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Asked about risk communication in general during the pandemic , Copes was effusive in his praise for British Columbia&amp;rsquo ; s Dr. Bonnie Henry . She benefits from being atop a coherently organized , well-managed public health system , something Ontario lacks , Copes said . But she&amp;rsquo ; s also a great communicator who&amp;rsquo ; s been given the space on most days to be B.C.&amp;rsquo ; s sole voice on scientific , technical and health matters . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Ontario , Copes said &amp;mdash ; and this predates the current government &amp;mdash ; politicians have a habit of putting themselves out front , even when that&amp;rsquo ; s not the best strategy . That&amp;rsquo ; s something , if he was still on the job , he would have advised against . &amp;ldquo ; How credible , ultimately , is a lay elected representative speaking about medical or scientific matters ? &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s true Williams himself isn&amp;rsquo ; t much of a speaker . But there&amp;rsquo ; s no reason Williams had to be the province&amp;rsquo ; s only , or even lead , expert voice on the pandemic . PHO used to have a deep roster of scientists who were both experts and experienced crisis communicators . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That hasn&amp;rsquo ; t been the case with COVID-19 . Many of those experts , including Crowcroft , have since left the agency . &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; ve done tons of this kind of stuff . If I would have been there , I&amp;rsquo ; m sure I would have been pulled into it , &amp;rdquo ; Crowcroft said . &amp;ldquo ; But it&amp;rsquo ; s not just about having the right person . You have to have the environment and the vision and the commitment to meet the mandate of the organization , which is protecting the health of Ontarians. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Several other senior leaders &amp;mdash ; in addition to Crowcroft , Martalog and Copes &amp;mdash ; have left the agency in the past year . PHO&amp;rsquo ; s former chief of health promotion , Dr. Brent Moloughney , is now Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s Associate Medical Officer of Health . His departure was a personal decision , he said . He wanted to be in Ottawa to be closer to his aging parents . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nicholas Paul , who as recently as January of this year , was PHO&amp;rsquo ; s laboratory operations director , was removed from the agency&amp;rsquo ; s online leadership chart sometime before March . He couldn&amp;rsquo ; t be reached for comment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; John McLaughlin , Crowcroft&amp;rsquo ; s predecessor as chief scientist , retired from PHO last year , on schedule , after turning 65. &amp;ldquo ; I regret seeing that other people have left , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; Sometimes there was illness , sometimes there was opportunity , but it seemed that just a coincidence of things has led to a lot of senior people not being there at a time like this . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are other , temporary , absences , too . Mike Mendaglio , the agency&amp;rsquo ; s chief laboratory operations officer , is on medical leave , as is Peter Donnelly , PHO&amp;rsquo ; s president and CEO . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Overall , according to PHO&amp;rsquo ; s organizational charts , the agency eliminated six leadership positions between June 2019 and January 2020 . Since then , at least two more senior leaders , Copes and Moloughney , have left the agency , while a third , Paul , no longer appears on the online version of the chart . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In an email , Janet Wong , a spokeswoman for the agency , said that , as &amp;ldquo ; with the majority of publicly funded organizations in Ontario , Public Health Ontario has had to streamline our operations to align with fiscal realities . &amp;rdquo ; That restructuring has led to the departure of some staff , she added . &amp;ldquo ; However , these staff changes have not impacted PHO&amp;rsquo ; s ability to respond to the pandemic. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Elliott&amp;rsquo ; s spokeswoman , Hayley Chazan , said PHO has served &amp;ldquo ; as a valued partner&amp;rdquo ; throughout the COVID-19 outbreak . &amp;ldquo ; We have benefited immensely from the advice and counsel from many of the organization&amp;rsquo ; s leaders , including Dr. Peter Donnelly , who helped lead the release of initial modelling , Dr. Shelley Deeks , who has helped develop our case and contact management plan , and Dr. Vanessa Allen , who is playing a key role in guiding Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s testing strategy and has also played a critical role in setting up our provincial laboratory network . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But that appreciation for the agency did not predate COVID-19 , according to multiple sources both inside and outside PHO. &amp;ldquo ; Certainly there was no love shown to public health in Ontario by the government , &amp;rdquo ; said Dr. Bob Bell , a medical doctor and health care administrator who served as Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s deputy minister of health and long-term care between 2014 and 2018. &amp;ldquo ; The funding cuts at Public Health Ontario can not have been useful to the response to COVID-19 . And when you look at the pennies saved compared to the dollars cost &amp;mdash ; that Ontario is going to suffer by delaying its reopening because of a lack of organized public health effectiveness &amp;mdash ; it&amp;rsquo ; s like , &amp;lsquo ; boy , was that ever stupid . &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some who have left the agency , meanwhile , believe the funding freeze and the institutional changes in the first years of the Ford administration may have compounded existing problems within the agency to such a degree that , in a year&amp;rsquo ; s time , PHO may not exist at all . &amp;ldquo ; Which would be a real shame because of all the effort that went in to creating it , &amp;rdquo ; said Crowcroft. &amp;ldquo ; And the reasons for needing it are still there . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On a certain level , the COVID pandemic is the just the bottom swing of a public health yo-yo that has happened over and over again in Ontario . &amp;ldquo ; You run in these circles where public health advocates get silenced gradually , and then there&amp;rsquo ; s a crisis . And then everyone goes &amp;lsquo ; Oh my God , what happened ? Why didn&amp;rsquo ; t we have the lab testing we needed ? Why didn&amp;rsquo ; t we have the right scientific advice ? Why was there no good public health leadership ? And it&amp;rsquo ; s like , &amp;lsquo ; Oh yeah , we shut that down , remember ? &amp;rsquo ; &amp;rdquo ; Crowcroft said . &amp;ldquo ; These aren&amp;rsquo ; t new stories . The United States stands with Canada in calling on Beijing for the immediate release of the two men and rejects the use of these unjustified detentions to coerce Canada , &amp;rdquo ; Pompeo said in a statement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Additionally , we echo Canada&amp;rsquo ; s call for immediate consular access to its two citizens , in accordance with the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations , as China has prohibited such access for almost six months , and the world has no knowledge of the two Canadians&amp;rsquo ; " " data-portal-copyright= " Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press " **28;5425;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78576146 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; OTTAWA &amp;mdash ; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s new auditor general says many audits have been cancelled or delayed &amp;ldquo ; indefinitely&amp;rdquo ; as her office faces budgetary constraints , as well as an increased workload due to COVID-19 and infrastructure spending . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have some audits that are ongoing that were expected to be tabled in the House in the fall of 2020 . We have delayed those into 2021 , &amp;rdquo ; Auditor General Karen Hogan told members of the federal finance committee on Monday . &amp;ldquo ; All other audits unfortunately at this time other than one audit , under the commissioner of the environment , have been put on hold , cancelled or delayed indefinitely so that we can focus on Investing in Canada and COVID-19. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The reasons for the setbacks are essentially twofold . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Firstly , the Office of the Auditor General ( OAG ) needs more money in order to fulfil its consistently growing mandate , said Hogan , who was appointed June 8 , to replace her predecessor Michael Ferguson , who died in February 2019. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last year , Ferguson told MPs that the office needed an extra $10.8 million in order to both hire new auditors and update the OAG&amp;rsquo ; s obsolete IT infrastructure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Now that the OAG has to audit Crown corporations as well as the federal government&amp;rsquo ; s $187-billion Investing in Canada infrastructure plan and COVID-19 aid measures , Hogan says she&amp;rsquo ; s going to need much more than that . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The $10.8 million is an outdated request&amp;hellip ; I think it&amp;rsquo ; s fair to even say it&amp;rsquo ; s a significantly outdated request , &amp;rdquo ; she explained , adding that her office is still calculating the new budget request and would submit it to parliamentarians soon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;5455;TOOLONG ... taps Karen Hogan to replace the late Michael Ferguson as auditor **28;5490;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;5520;TOOLONG ... auditor general says lack of funds leaving him with outdated technology , not enough **27;5555;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p ... Secondly , the aforementioned Investing in Canada and COVID-19 audits are so large in scope , they will likely take years to complete fully and will consume much of the OAG&amp;rsquo ; s resources , Hogan warned . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A unanimous motion adopted by members of the finance committee earlier this month asked the OAG to audit all federal programs association to the pandemic. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Auditing all of the COVID programs would be astronomical , &amp;rdquo ; Hogan said , adding it would take many years and wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t be in the best interests of Parliament or Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , Hogan said her office is going to prioritize programs according to &amp;ldquo ; risk&amp;rdquo ; and where she thinks audits will have &amp;ldquo ; the best impact and value . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The first parts of the government&amp;rsquo ; s pandemic response plan being audited are the availability of personal protective equipment , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s food supply , and the Canada Emergency Response Benefit , a subsidy to help Canadians who lost their jobs or had their hours cut by the pandemic . The subsidy , which provides $2,000-a-month to individuals , is budgeted to cost the government $60 billion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Conservative finance critic Pierre Poilievre said Parliament is eager for answers , but MPs also want the auditor general to do a thorough job . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt; -- With files from Canadian Press&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;* Email : &lt;a href= " **27;5584;TOOLONG " **34;5613;TOOLONG Twitter : &lt;a href= " https : **25;5649;TOOLONG " class= " twitter-follow-button " &gt;ChrisGNardi &; ... &lt;/p&gt; Christopher NardiTue , 23 Jun 2020 01:09:55 **45;5676;TOOLONG ... Police said Horace&amp;rsquo ; s family was in the home at the time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; CTV quoted a neighbour who heard one gun shot and saw the men leave in two cars . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Paramedics took the victim to hospital , where he was pronounced dead . Police in London said they do not believe this was a random incident , but said nothing about why Horace , who lived in Toronto , may have been specifically targeted . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The London Police Service has received several media inquiries about the identity of the deceased and possible historical association to National Patriotic Front in Liberia . &amp;nbsp ; The London Police Service is aware of these inquiries , but can not confirm this fact at this time , &amp;rdquo ; a statement said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Several media outlets , in Canada and Africa , identified Horace as the former leader of a rebel militia fighting the brutal war in Liberia and Sierra Leone in the 1990s. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canadian journalist and historian Michael Petrou was among those who drew the link on Twitter . Bill Horace and his men were passing . They entered the plantation and accused us of looting the place . He then ordered his men to arrest people . They started chasing us , and everybody was running all over the place . They then started firing at us . I first saw one woman fall . The bullet hit her on the head . Her husband was crying . Then one of the other fighters shot him also . Both of them died instantly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two years later , in 2012 , it emerged Canada was formally investigating Horace for war crimes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That same year , the former president of Liberia and leader of the NPFL , Charles Taylor , was convicted at the United Nations-backed Special Court for Sierra Leone for planning , aiding and abetting war crimes , some of the worst in recorded history . He said , long-term , airlines still have fixed costs and they will become more and more unmanageable if planes stay grounded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; As long as these restrictions stay in place and we are not looking at balanced ways of reopening the economy , it will have a tremendous impact on the financial viability of these businesses . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Currently , with a few exceptions , only Canadian citizens and permanent residents are allowed to enter the country . Government relations director Howard Liebman , with Air Transat , said his company can&amp;rsquo ; t wait until the virus goes away . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We can&amp;rsquo ; t wait years until there is a widely available vaccine to get back in the air . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have not operated or sold tickets in more than three months , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; There is no business or industry that can go for three months without revenue or operations . &amp;rdquo ; " data-portal-copyright= " Provincial Archives of Alberta " **28;6792;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78576020 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; EDMONTON &amp;mdash ; Alberta is considering severing its contract with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police , a move that would require the creation &amp;mdash ; or , rather , re-creation &amp;mdash ; of a provincial police force . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the province&amp;rsquo ; s 115-year history until right now , the RCMP &amp;mdash ; or its precursor , the North-West Mounted Police &amp;mdash ; has provided policing services for much of Alberta , particularly rural areas and small towns . But in the wake of recommendations from a panel seeking out ideas on a &amp;ldquo ; fair deal&amp;rdquo ; for Alberta within confederation , the province may consider creating its own police force , as it did for roughly 15 years around the time of the First World War . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Between 1917 and 1932 , Alberta was policed by the Alberta Provincial Police . The force came to be mainly because the RCMP&amp;rsquo ; s ranks were being drained by the war effort . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But , according to the work of Sean Moir , an Edmonton historian cited in a 2007 &lt;em&gt;Edmonton Journal&lt;/em&gt; article , and corroborated from historical newspaper clippings of the time , there was another reason : The RCMP didn&amp;rsquo ; t want to police Prohibition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;6822;TOOLONG ... says Alberta should consider ditching CPP , RCMP ; Kenney considers **28;6857;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;6887;TOOLONG ... video shows RCMP tackling and punching Alberta chief Allan Adam in **27;6922;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p ... Prohibition had come into effect across the country by 1918 . But provinces had put in their own liquor bans prior to that , along with some municipalities and counties under the 1878 Canada Temperance Act . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; My argument is that these guys had gone through it before and they knew what it was going to be like to enforce very unpopular liquor legislation . They knew it was going to be a no-win situation , &amp;rdquo ; Moir told the **28;6951;TOOLONG . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An April 1918 &lt;a href= " http : **34;6981;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " rel= " noopener " &gt;newspaper clipping&lt;/a&gt; from the Edmonton Bulletin newspaper , on the debate over a provincial police force , cites Alberta Premier Charles Stewart as saying the &amp;ldquo ; Red Coats&amp;rdquo ; had no desire to enforce Prohibition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Even when Prohibition ended &amp;mdash ; the first day the taps ran in Alberta was May 12 , 1924 &amp;mdash ; the Alberta Provincial Police stuck around . Until the Great Depression hit . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;7017;TOOLONG ... title= " In the province 's 115-year history until right now , the RCMP -- or its precursor , the North-West Mounted Police -- has provided policing services for much of Alberta . " alt= " In the province 's 115-year history until right now , the RCMP -- or its precursor , the North-West Mounted Police -- has provided policing services for much of Alberta . " data-portal-copyright= " Global News via Postmedia/File " **28;7052;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78576031 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 1930 , Premier John Brownlee asked politicians for ideas on how to save money that would not affect services . The proposal made by Conservative leader David Duggan was to scrap the police and bring in the RCMP , for savings of $250,000 per year ( about $3.7 million in today&amp;rsquo ; s dollars ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Duggan&amp;rsquo ; s proposal failed , but by 1932 the economics had deteriorated sufficiently , and legislators reinstated the Dominion government&amp;rsquo ; s police force . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The current 20-year contract , signed in 2011 under then-Alberta Premier Ed Stelmach , goes until 2032 . The province can still withdraw from the contract , provided it gives the federal government two year&amp;rsquo ; s notice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The argument today for a provincial force are rising crime rates in rural areas of the province , lengthy response times to 911 calls , staffing and western alienation issues . The Fair Deal panel says a local force would be better positioned to serve Albertans. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A stable police service that allowed members to stay grounded in local communities would be attractive to men and women considering law enforcement as a career , &amp;rdquo ; the report says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still , the panel warned that there would be cost issues associated with taking over the policing duties of the RCMP &amp;mdash ; just as there were a century ago . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alberta pays roughly $262 million per year for the RCMP , with the federal government contributing $112 million per year . " data-portal-copyright= " Ernest Doroszuk/Toronto Sun/Postmedia " **28;7940;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78575742 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; A corrupt Toronto police officer was part of a criminal organization that used stolen encrypted police radios to unfairly profit in southern Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s lucrative and dangerous tow truck wars , police said Monday . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Eleven people were arrested in the anti-corruption and organized crime probe , including a police constable and seven tow truck drivers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The constable was so entrenched in a towing cartel he not only profited by sharing police equipment and information , he also owned a car rental service and two tow trucks being operated by members of the group , police alleged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A police radio decrypts private communications between officers , allowing users to listen in . A consortium of tow truck drivers could then be the first to learn of traffic collisions and arrive at the scene to solicit towing business and other services , police said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Several tow truck employees from three different towing companies had access to three stolen Toronto police radios , at least one of which was stolen from police by a police officer , Supt. Domenic Sinopoli alleged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Three radios were recovered &amp;mdash ; one of which went missing in February 2018 , suggesting the scheme may have operated for more than two years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Highlighting the organization of the towing consortium , collision information from the radios was distributed using an internet app to other tow drivers who paid a monthly subscription fee . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The industry is rife with corruption , &amp;rdquo ; Sinopoli said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Toronto police&amp;rsquo ; s Professional Standards Unit , which internally monitors the ethics and integrity of its members , started investigating theft of police radios last August . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; As the investigation took on some life , the corruption revealed itself , &amp;rdquo ; said Sinopoli. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; What we learned was a consortium of tow trucks were in possession of stolen police radios and were utilizing the encrypted transmissions to facilitate their business interests . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The arrested officer , Const . Ronald Joseph , 47 , of Toronto , who has been with Toronto police for 11 years , allegedly helped members of the consortium get a genuine police radio , which was then cloned and the cloned version checked back in with police . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He used his position to steal and transfer a police radio that would give advantage to the group with respect to the ability to intercept police communication , attend more accidents or perhaps evade police detection , &amp;rdquo ; Sinopoli alleged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;7970;TOOLONG ... title= " A policeman executes a search warrant in relation to Toronto 's tow truck war . " alt= " A policeman executes a search warrant in relation to Toronto 's tow truck war . " data-portal-copyright= " York Regional Police " **28;8005;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78575749 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Joseph is also accused of being paid for telling the group of accident locations as well as profiting from tows and rentals from his own business interests . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The officer would receive monetary compensation for the tow trucks , he would receive kickbacks for the tips he provided and he would receive referrals to his car rental agency , &amp;rdquo ; said Sinopoli. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Toronto police knew Joseph owned a car rental service but were unaware of his ownership of tow trucks , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The scheme started to unravel in May , when officers stopped a tow truck driver on Highway 400 . The officers found a genuine Toronto police radio in the tow truck , Sinopoli said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The driver , Kevin Lima , 27 , of Barrie , Ont. , was charged with dangerous driving and released at the scene . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Police discovered the radio had the same identification as a radio at 22 Division . When officers examined the radio still being used by police officers , it was found to be a clone , meaning a replica that looks and acts like the real thing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A few weeks later , police searched several homes in Toronto , Barrie and Brampton and found a second Toronto police radio , reported lost or stolen from 14 Division . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Also found were numerous other radios that appear to be from other organizations , possibly police agencies , and parts used for cloning radios , police said . Sinopoli said organizations will need to come in and try to identify their radios . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Then , on June 9 , three tow truck drivers arrived at the Costco parking lot near the busy highway intersection of Highway 401 and Allen Rd. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Police found a third Toronto police radio and a loaded 9mm handgun , Sinopoli said . All three were arrested . Lima was one of them , along with Jacob Villeneuve Portela , 21 , of Toronto , and Giuseppe Carfora , 27 , of Guelph. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; More police searches came on Thursday , at five homes and seven businesses in southern and northern Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Along with the 11 arrests police seized six tow trucks , a loaded handgun and $35,000 cash , police said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Joseph worked in 22 Division , in the city&amp;rsquo ; s west-end , that includes a stretch of the busy Gardiner Expressway . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sinopoli said Joseph&amp;rsquo ; s link to the group appears to be through a business relationship with Lima . The answer will sketch the outline of Canadian life in the months ahead . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; New research suggests , though , that certain cities are far more susceptible to the virus than others . The findings could be crucial for public health officials planning for a possible resurgence of the virus . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think we can safely say that certain drivers , such as a dense way of living , as well as age structure , in particular , the share of the population living in nursing homes , will strongly continue to predict worse outcomes , &amp;rdquo ; said Klaus Desmet , an economist at Southern Methodist University , Texas , in an interview with the National Post . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For months , experts have been tracking the capricious path of the new coronavirus . It left an appalling trail of destruction in Italy , killing nearly 35,000 people , and then hit Germany with a glancing blow and a quarter of the deaths that Italy experienced . New York City suffered one of the worst outbreaks in the world while Los Angeles suffered a death toll one-sixth the size . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Canada , greater Toronto and Montreal account for more than 66,000 of the roughly 100,000 cases , while the rest of Canada accounts for the rest . Desmet says it&amp;rsquo ; s likely that Canada&amp;rsquo ; s largest two cities fell victim to the same characteristics as New York City . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; What we find is that large metropolis are vulnerable mainly for two reasons . First , they are places with a dense way of life . Second , in large urban areas it is very hard to create a disease-free bubble because there is always inflow and outflow , &amp;rdquo ; said Desmet. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;8383;TOOLONG ... pandemic prompts urbanites to rethink ' grand bargain ' of dense city **27;8418;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;8447;TOOLONG ... in one day : Sunday saw the biggest-ever daily increase in new COVID-19 **26;8482;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p &; ... By isolating each variable , Desmet and Romain Wacziarg , an economist at the University of California , Los Angeles , have found that a city&amp;rsquo ; s density is a huge factor , along with the age of the population and its distance to an international airport . Most importantly , the researchers believe that these characteristics are likely to define the shape of the outbreak in the future . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The evidence so far suggests the severity of the disease will not equal out across cities , but remain uneven and with some cities grappling with persistent outbreaks while others remain relatively calm . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If this trend continues , it means officials can concentrate resources in areas with the highest susceptibility without fearing that other areas will be left vulnerable to their own outbreak . It also means certain places can have less stringent lockdowns and earlier reopenings without the risk of overwhelming the health care systems . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;8510;TOOLONG ... title= " Passengers wearing protective masks ride a streetcar in Toronto on June 18. " data-portal-copyright= " Stephanie Foden/Bloomberg " **28;8545;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78575428 " /&gt; &lt;h3&gt;Density and public **25;8575;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; The most obvious guess about what drives the severity of an outbreak is density . Anyone skimming the list of cities particularly affected by COVID-19 will see a list of North America&amp;rsquo ; s most dense cities . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This should come as no surprise : as with any other infectious disease , contact between susceptible and infected individuals is a key determinant of the spread of the disease , &amp;rdquo ; reads a study from Desmet and Wacziarg on the differences in COVID-19 outbreaks across the United States . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study considers several features of density , including the share of individuals living in multi-unit housing structures and the number of people per household . Another factor measures the amount of density a random person in the city or county will encounter in a square kilometre . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The researchers found multi-unit housing and the size of households are both positively associated with cases and deaths , and they expect this to be a feature of any future outbreak . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The research also found that places with more people using public transit have much worse COVID-19 outbreaks , particularly in terms of deaths . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Any epidemiological model of infectious disease will tell you that one of the most important drivers of the spread of the disease is the infection rate . Obviously that infection rate depends on how many other people an infected individual bumps into every day ( and ) that&amp;rsquo ; ll be much larger if I use the metro than if I live on an isolated farm on the countryside , &amp;rdquo ; said Desmet. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;8602;TOOLONG ... title= " Terminal 1 at Toronto 's Pearson Airport on June 18. " alt= " Terminal 1 at Toronto 's Pearson Airport on June 18. " data-portal-copyright= " Peter J. Thompson / National Post " **28;8637;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78575422 " /&gt; **29;8667;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced in March that international flights would only be arriving in Vancouver , Calgary , Toronto and Montreal , which provided laboratory conditions for measuring the effects of international travel on the pandemic. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the United States , the researchers also found a clear correlation between a city&amp;rsquo ; s distance to an international airport and an early outbreak of COVID-19. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There is a randomness in locations that got the virus early . One important exception is the variable capturing distance to international airports with connections to the top-5 COVID incidence countries as of March 15 , &amp;rdquo ; the study reports . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Toronto , the higher infection rates clustered around the airport . Peel Region , which is home to Pearson International Airport , has a rate of 328 cases per 100,000 people . That&amp;rsquo ; s one of the highest rates in the province , second only to the city of Toronto itself , which has 394 cases per 100,000 people . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This could also be what drove some small differences in case numbers in Alberta . In Calgary , where the airport remained open to international flights , the infection rates surged ahead of Edmonton , where the airport is smaller , farther away from the city and closed to international travel . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s almost certain that cities close to international airports get infected earlier than others , but Desmet said it&amp;rsquo ; s less clear whether they will be worse off in the long run . The evidence does seem to be pointing in that direction , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h3&gt;Age of population&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; Interestingly , the researchers found that if a county has more people over the age of 75 , it is likely to have fewer cases . This is likely because younger people are more likely to take part in activities that spread the virus , like large social gatherings and events . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Places with a large share of retired individuals may feature fewer places ( bars , stadiums ) where the disease spreads rapidly , &amp;rdquo ; the study says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And although an older population tends to be associated with lower transmission , in some situations it can lead to more deaths . This could also be driven by outbreaks at nursing homes , which have seen horrifying death rates . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This finding is consistent with the idea that once a county is affected by the pandemic , its nursing homes can quickly become powderkegs , and account for larger shares of countywide deaths . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;8698;TOOLONG ... title= " The line for Zara 's Queen Street West location in Toronto on June 15. " alt= " The line for Zara 's Queen Street West location in Toronto on June 15. " data-portal-copyright= " Peter J. Thompson / National Post " **28;8733;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78575423 " /&gt; &lt;h3&gt;Other factors&lt;/h3&gt; &lt;p&gt; The researchers found that some widely hypothesized risk factors for COVID-19 may not be that important . For example , the share of smokers and obese people does not seem to be a big driver of high mortality rates . Even the quality of health care infrastructure seems to be much less important than other factors like the density of the city and the age of the population . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although a person&amp;rsquo ; s level of education itself seems to have little bearing on the severity of an outbreak , poverty and inequality seem to be big drivers . Poverty has a strong bearing on the mortality rate and inequality correlates with more cases of COVID-19. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the United States , race also matters a great deal . Outbreaks are more severe in areas with more Black and Hispanic people , both in terms of the number of cases and deaths . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Overall , these results confirm concerns that the COVID-19 pandemic has a disparate effect on various racial groups , &amp;rdquo ; the paper reads . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; All of these trends are important , but they aren&amp;rsquo ; t the final story . For instance , the fact that New Jersey is right beside New York is far more influential to its outbreak potential than any state-specific characteristics . Likewise , the fact that Hawaii is a remote island is a much better predictor than any other characteristic . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study also emphasizes one of the most vexing features of a virus outbreak , that so many of the activities that make for a happy life now put people at an increased risk . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Taken together , being connected to many other people makes you vulnerable . " data-portal-copyright= " GUILLERMO ARIAS/AFP via Getty Images " **28;9506;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78574652 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; OTTAWA &amp;ndash ; Canadian experts looking at a surge of new COVID-19 cases in several U.S. states say it should be a warning to Canada , but not a cause for alarm . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Several U.S. states have seen huge spikes in COVID-19 cases in the past weeks . On Friday , Arizona reported 3,217 new cases of the disease and Florida saw 4,049 . In California , there were 4,351 cases , Texas saw 4,189 and Georgia saw 1,800 new cases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; All of these states have seen numbers higher than they have seen at any point in the pandemic , which is coming weeks after they allowed restaurants , businesses and even theatres to open up again . In many cases those businesses opened without the same distance requirements that are common in Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Theresa Tam , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s chief public health officer , said they are following the situation south of the border closely and it should serve as a cautionary tale . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We do see all of these kinds of trends as a warning signal for us again , reminding Canadians the virus is still around , very much around in many parts of the world including the U.S , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said failing to maintain high standards around hand-washing and social distancing could quickly cause a surge in new infections . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We need to keep up and the moment we let go this virus could find some way of accelerating in our community . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The provincial and federal governments came to an agreed set of guidelines for reopening that ensured cases were on a downward trend before a province reopened and that contact tracing and testing were available . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Georgia , one of the states now seeing a surge , was one of the first U.S. states to open its economy on April 24 . On that day , when businesses reopened in the state there were 608 new cases reported , a month ago it had risen to 946 and as of Friday there were 1,800 cases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Florida , Arizona , California , and Texas all began their reopening efforts in early May and are now seeing daily case counts that are two or three times as high as at any point in the pandemic. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ontario and Quebec , Canada&amp;rsquo ; s worst hit provinces , have started their reopening plans , but they have done so regionally and gradually compared to the U.S. states . Toronto and Montreal , which were particularly hard hit , still have many restrictions in place . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ontario saw 175 new cases on Sunday , while Quebec saw just 92. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Zain Chagla , a specialist in infectious diseases and an assistant professor at McMaster University , said everything he has seen from the U.S. indicates they simply opened up too fast . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;9536;TOOLONG ... class= " alignleft size-full wp-image-78575512 " src= " https : **33;9571;TOOLONG ... alt= " " width= " 1001 " height= " 583 " srcset= " https : **31;9606;TOOLONG ... 1001w , https : **39;9639;TOOLONG ... 150w , https : **39;9680;TOOLONG ... 300w , https : **39;9721;TOOLONG ... 768w " sizes= " ( max-width : 1001px ) 100vw , 1001px " &gt;&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We saw a preview of what not to do in the United States is not just wait till you get a peak , let the cases drop a little bit and then open the door . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said there was clearly still community transmission in these states when the decision was made to reopen and the virus has been able to rapidly spread . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Moving slower is probably a whole lot better than moving faster , as we&amp;rsquo ; re seeing in the United States . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Chagla said Canadian provinces have moved from complete lockdowns to gradual reopenings , which has given them the opportunity to address new outbreaks and clusters before they spread . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re opening the door much later into our downward curve . " That 's the question we put to doctors , scientists , philosophers , psychologists , futurists , microbiologists and bioethicists , 100 days after the World Health Organization officially declared COVID-19 a global pandemic . We asked the experts what they 're anticipating for the next 100 days , what we should do differently , what worries them most . " Things have changed at such manic speed in the past three months , it 's difficult to predict what the next 100 days will yield , " said McGill University 's Samuel Veissi ? re . Below , Veissi ? re and others reflect on the challenges ahead . Their responses have been edited for clarity and length . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;On compliance fatigue , social isolation and the politics of a pandemic : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m worried about future waves being imminent , maybe not even waves , but just this steady , persistent ( viral activity ) . &amp;nbsp ; How do we sustain what we&amp;rsquo ; re doing ? It&amp;rsquo ; s so important for mental health to have livelihoods . To continue to function . I don&amp;rsquo ; t know what the answer is . That kind of keeps me awake . &amp;rdquo ; &amp;nbsp ; &amp;mdash ; &lt;em ... Samira Mubareka , virologist and infectious diseases doctor at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; As summer arrives , lockdown-weary people will increasingly flock to parks , beaches . Protest rallies and , south of the border , political rallies will bring people together in large numbers . This could prolong the current wave of infection or even spur a second wave . Paradoxically , efforts to combat one social problem ( protest rallies to combat racism ) could exacerbate another social problem ( the spread of COVID-19 ) &amp;hellip ; . Unlike the 1918 flu pandemic , in which the sight of coffins was an everyday occurrence , COVID-19 is largely a hidden pandemic , where the sick and dying are sequestered in hospitals , and coffins are nowhere to be seen . This can lead people to underestimate the seriousness of the current pandemic. &amp;rdquo ; &amp;mdash ; &lt;em&gt;Dr . Steven Taylor , professor and clinical psychologist at the University of British Columbia&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Politics and social polarization is what worries me the most . Before the pandemic some of us had predicted that 2020 would be the year of reason and reconciliation in the culture wars . We couldn&amp;rsquo ; t have been more wrong . For a few weeks , as the world ground to a halt , trying to make sense of the new threat posed by the virus , people everywhere appeared to be uniting in ways never seen before . This sadly didn&amp;rsquo ; t last . As everything from epidemiology , mathematical modelling , mask wearing , treatment options and whether or not to lock down became politicized , the already-polarized left-right divide took a sharper turn toward irreconcilable divisions . PoliticsNewsGovernment COVID-19 emergency measures are ' death of civil liberties by a thousand cuts ' : reporthttp : **34;11540;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **33;11576;TOOLONG ... title= " Park-goers at Trinity-Bellwoods Park in Toronto , after the city painted it with more than a hundred social distancing circles . " alt= " Park-goers at Trinity-Bellwoods Park in Toronto , after the city painted it with more than a hundred social distancing circles . " data-portal-copyright= " Jack Boland/Postmedia/File " **28;11611;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78573829 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; OTTAWA &amp;mdash ; The many emergency laws and regulations introduced to target the COVID-19 pandemic have amounted to the &amp;ldquo ; death of civil liberties by a thousand cuts , &amp;rdquo ; a new report says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The non-profit Canadian Civil Liberties Association ( CCLA ) on Friday released a lengthy document that reviews emergency measures introduced by federal , provincial and municipal levels of government in recent months , which authorized everything from unlimited spending powers to hefty fines for people who fail to practise social distancing . The organization asserts that those measures amount to a broad overreach of government powers that , left unchecked , threatens to become permanent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The pandemic has led to a thousand impositions on civil liberties that might feel minor alone , but which taken together represent an extraordinary change to civil liberties in Canada , &amp;rdquo ; the report said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Limits to civil liberties include government-led initiatives to curb &amp;ldquo ; misinformation , &amp;rdquo ; mandatory masks or temperature checks in private settings , restricted access to public settings , or even attempts to hinder &amp;ldquo ; drive-in religious services , &amp;rdquo ; the report said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Each of these constrain freedoms in what some might consider small ways . But taken together , they indicate a major shift in Canada towards a more designated , circumscribed , and government-ordered way of doing things . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study underscores the deep divisions that have surfaced in recent months , as the public grapples with the extent to which government should control public life in the name of safety . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hefty fines issued by municipal police to people walking their dogs , for example , has been called an unnecessary overreach by some , while others argue that those fines might be seen as part of a broader need for compliance in order to curb the spread of the virus . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;11641;TOOLONG ... just passed 100,000 COVID-19 cases . 8,257 of those have been **26;11676;TOOLONG &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;11704;TOOLONG ... contact tracing app ready to be tested in Ontario : **28;11739;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt; ... The CCLA report does not outright dismiss the need for emergency measures to combat COVID-19 , but said the inconsistent and sometimes illogical nature of those policies likely reduced their effectiveness , while also restricting civil liberties . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Bill 10 , introduced by Alberta Premier Jason Kenney in response to the pandemic , &amp;ldquo ; allows a single minister to exercise the awesome lawmaking power of a parliamentary majority for up to 6 months after the end of the emergency , &amp;rdquo ; for example , while Ontario and Quebec &amp;ldquo ; wove a dragnet of social distancing rules&amp;rdquo ; enforced through punitive fines. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the effectiveness and necessity of those sweeping powers remains unclear , the report said , while blatant policy shortfalls caused a high rate of deaths in seniors&amp;rsquo ; homes and in some cases a failure to provide safe haven for vulnerable populations . The city of Toronto , the report said , &amp;ldquo ; dragged its feet on ensuring that there were adequate and safe housing solutions for people experiencing homelessness. &amp;rdquo ; Homeless people were &amp;rdquo ; always an afterthought for leadership , at best , &amp;rdquo ; the CCLA said , as were minority populations like Indigenous . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The CCLA rated a number of measures introduced by the various orders of government , giving an &amp;ldquo ; F&amp;rdquo ; grade to Alberta&amp;rsquo ; s B-10 for being &amp;ldquo ; radically **26;11769;TOOLONG ; to the threat of the pandemic . Nunavut&amp;rsquo ; s initial public restrictions received a &amp;ldquo ; D&amp;rdquo ; but was later raised to a &amp;ldquo ; B+&amp;rdquo ; after the territorial government scaled back some of those limits . A decision by the Newfoundland government to close its border to non-residents received an &amp;ldquo ; F&amp;rdquo ; for its direct infringement on rights to movement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study&amp;rsquo ; s conclusion calls on governments to lift emergency restrictions as soon as possible . It also argues that the public must begin to contemplate the way in which civil liberties improve public life overall , even if it comes at the expense of convenience or health in some cases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We can not pretend anymore that there is some elusive balance between civil liberties and public health to be found , &amp;rdquo ; it said . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; Our civil liberties inform our public health , as much as antibody levels and body temperature . " data-portal-copyright= " Photo illustration " **28;12015;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78573770 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; OTTAWA &amp;ndash ; Former diplomats say China&amp;rsquo ; s decision to charge two Canadians with espionage , after detaining them for more than 18 months , should be a wake-up call to the Trudeau government to stop the soft diplomacy and play hardball. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Chinese prosecutors announced Friday that Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor would be charged with espionage . Their arrests in 2018 came shortly after Canadian officials detained Huawei executive , Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said the arrests and charges remain arbitrary and without merit and he is disappointed China continues to detain the two men . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have continued to express our disappointment with the Chinese decision , with the Chinese detention of these two Canadians . We will continue to advocate for their release , for their return to Canada , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian said each is charged with &amp;ldquo ; secretly gathering state secrets for overseas forces with particularly serious consequences . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s former ambassador to China , Guy Saint-Jacques , said the soft diplomacy strategy the Trudeau government has taken has failed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The federal government has to come to the conclusion that the appeasement strategy that has been followed so far , has produced no result . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Saint-Jacques said the government should consider trade sanctions and being more aggressive with Chinese interference in Canada . It could also finally announce Huawei won&amp;rsquo ; t have access to Canada&amp;rsquo ; s 5G telecom network . Canada should also advocate other countries&amp;nbsp ; adopt such measures to leverage the pressure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s the kind of behaviour we have to prevent going into the future . We are a small player for China , but I think we can exact a price especially when we&amp;rsquo ; re working with others . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kovrig and Spavor have been held with very limited consular contacts in a Chinese prison since their arrest in late 2018 . Chinese Ambassador to Canada Cong Peiwu said in an interview with Reuters last week that consular services for Kovrig and Spavor had been suspended due to coronavirus-control measures earlier this year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meng by contrast has been on a form of house arrest since her detention began , allowed to move between two Vancouver mansions while wearing an ankle bracelet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;12045;TOOLONG ... title= " Huawei Chief Financial Officer , Meng Wanzhou , leaves B.C. " data-portal-copyright= " Don MacKinnon/AFP via Getty Images " **28;12080;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 78545470 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meng recently lost a court decision in her extradition case . She faces fraud charges in the United States and was arrested at the American&amp;rsquo ; s request while transiting through the Vancouver airport . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Saint-Jacques said the recent loss in Canadian courts was likely the catalyst for the criminal charges against Kovrig and Spavor. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The Chinese must come to the conclusion that the extraction process will drag on for years and they decided to up the ante by launching the formal trial , &amp;rdquo ; said Saint-Jacques. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Robert Malley , president of the International Crisis Group , the conflict resolution organization Kovrig works for , said the charges against him were &amp;ldquo ; completely baseless&amp;rdquo ; and &amp;ldquo ; groundless. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said that Kovrig was &amp;ldquo ; open and transparent&amp;rdquo ; in his work , and Chinese officials have not provided any evidence to suggest otherwise . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s deeply disappointing , but it&amp;rsquo ; s wholly unsurprising , &amp;rdquo ; Malley said . &amp;ldquo ; From the very beginning , this has been a political case , not a legal one . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 360 " src= " https : **34;12110;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;12146;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; Trudeau was asked if he viewed the two men as hostages , which he did not answer . He also didn&amp;rsquo ; t outline any more aggressive measures to garner their release . He said a lot was being done behind the scenes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We are using a wide range of public and private measures to ensure that everything is being done to get the Michaels home . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said Chinese officials clearly believe the Meng case is politically motivated , but his government has been clear that the judicial system in Canada is independent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The Chinese authorities have directly linked the case of the two Michaels to the case of Ms. Meng , which is extremely disappointing because for us it is not , there are no links . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Earlier this week , Zhao , the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman , denounced the legal proceedings against Meng as an &amp;ldquo ; outright political case with grave consequences , &amp;rdquo ; adding that Canada had been acting as a U.S. &amp;ldquo ; accomplice&amp;rdquo ; to oppress Chinese technology companies . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Asked Friday for the Chinese government&amp;rsquo ; s position on &amp;ldquo ; hostage diplomacy , &amp;rdquo ; Zhao rejected the question as &amp;ldquo ; vicious . &amp;rdquo ; &amp;ldquo ; Ask the Canadian government what &amp;lsquo ; hostage diplomacy&amp;rsquo ; is , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Charles Burton , an associate professor at Brock University and former counsellor at the Canadian Embassy in China , said Kovrig and Spavor should not expect a fair trial . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The case has already been developed , it&amp;rsquo ; s very likely that they will be found guilty of these serious charges , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; The trial itself , because it impinges on national security matters , would probably only amount to half a day . And we wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t have any access to the proceedings . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What China calls the People&amp;rsquo ; s Procuratorate investigated and will prosecute the case , which Burton said effectively means the government will decide the men&amp;rsquo ; s guilt and their sentence . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They don&amp;rsquo ; t have the principle of judicial independence . And therefore these decisions are made by the Chinese Communist Party . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Burton said the government approach has been to not antagonize China , but that clearly isn&amp;rsquo ; t delivering . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Our policy has been to make concessions to the Chinese regime , in hope that it puts them favourably disposed to listen to our increasingly desperate pleas for release of Kovrig and Spavor from the hell that they&amp;rsquo ; ve been experiencing now for 557 days . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said taking a tougher stance won&amp;rsquo ; t necessarily mean retaliation from China , especially if the government builds up a coalition of countries prepared to take a unified stance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If there&amp;rsquo ; s political will to really stand up and make a strong indication to China that violations of the international rules based order , through their hostage diplomacy tactics are simply unacceptable to Canada , then that might lead to China rethinking how they&amp;rsquo ; re approaching Canada . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt; -- with files from Reuters and Washington Post&lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;em&gt;* Email : &lt;a href= " **29;12182;TOOLONG " **36;12213;TOOLONG Twitter : &lt;a class= " twitter-follow-button " href= " https : **25;12251;TOOLONG " &gt; **32;12278;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; Ryan TumiltyFri , 19 Jun 2020 23:41:48 **45;12312;TOOLONG ... PoliticsNewsWorldDozens of puppies found dead in cargo hold of Ukraine plane that landed in Torontohttp : **33;12359;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **33;12394;TOOLONG ... title= " Planes of the Ukrainian International airlines at the Kyiv Boryspil International Airport in Ukraine . Van Hoepen&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A grisly scene unfolded Saturday as a Ukraine International Airlines flight cargo hold was being emptied in Toronto ; 38 puppies dead from apparent suffocation. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ukraine Airlines flight PS 1241 landed at Pearson International Airport on June 13 , carrying 500 puppies in the cargo hold that were meant to be sold in the Toronto area , according to a statement by the &lt;a href= " https : **33;12459;TOOLONG ... Food Inspection Agency&lt;/a&gt; ( CFIA ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A source recalls seeing the puppies in Ukraine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There were around 500 total , 200 French bulldogs included , that were taken for transportation on the &lt;a href= " https : //kbp.aero/en/ " &gt;Borispol&lt;/a ... flight , including 300 cages , which meant some cages contained two dogs , &amp;rdquo ; the source said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The temperatures at the time of loading was over 30 C , and the puppies were visibly suffering according to eyewitness accounts , with multiple crates being placed on top of each other , and some even being encased in plastic . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **33;12494;TOOLONG ... title= " Screen grab from a video taken by a freight worker at Kyiv Boryspil International Airport showing crates containing live animals stacked high awaiting to be loaded in the airplane.
